name: Design mistakes in earlier simulators
maintainer: Synthesised from: BUET group (DhakaSim/RoadBird: Mushfiq, Toha, Salim, Mostak, Rahaman, Al-Nabhan, Sadri, Al Islam); Technical University of Crete TrafficFluid ERC project (Troullinos, Chalkiadakis, Manolis, Papamichail, Papageorgiou); IIT Bombay Transportation Lab (SiMTraM); Dustin Carlino (A/B Street); Prof. Ashish Verma, IISc IST Lab (review of the 2026 Hebbal microsimulation study); FHWA Traffic Analysis Toolbox Vol. III; Indian PCU literature
first_release: Evidence spans 2013 (SiMTraM last SourceForge update) to 2026 (IISc review of Hebbal study, report dated 10 Aug 2026)
last_activity: 2026 (IISc technical review of 'Integrated Traffic Microsimulation Study - Bengaluru, Hebbal Flyover & Hebbal Short Tunnel'); TrafficFluid-Sim user manual May 2025
licence: Not applicable to a lesson. Related code: SiMTraM GPLv3; A/B Street Apache-2.0; TrafficFluid-Sim open source but licence not named on project page [uncertain]; DhakaSim/RoadBird code availability not stated [uncertain]
language: Not applicable. Related: DhakaSim Java and C++ (per DhakaSim research page snippet) [uncertain]; TrafficFluid-Sim C++ (SUMO fork, C/C++ plugin API); A/B Street Rust
code_availability: SiMTraM: Windows binary zip on SourceForge (SiMTraM-0.1.1-winbin.zip). TrafficFluid-Sim: source at github.com/trafficfluid-dssl/trafficfluid-sim plus Windows/Ubuntu 22.04 binaries. A/B Street: github.com/a-b-street/abstreet. DhakaSim/RoadBird: paper and project site; public repository not found [uncertain].
maintenance_health: SiMTraM last updated 2013-04-29 with 0 weekly downloads: effectively abandoned. TrafficFluid-Sim is pinned to SUMO commit 6c09f092 of 20 Oct 2020 and still documented on that base in May 2025, i.e. about 4.5 years of upstream drift. A/B Street's author wrote an 'Almost Postmortem' and later split the monolith into smaller tools under A/B Street Ltd. DhakaSim was superseded by RoadBird (2020).
known_limitations: This lesson set is drawn mostly from author self-reports and one expert review, not from a systematic survey. Several items (static PCU, lane-based models on Indian roads) rest on conference papers whose full texts were only partially read. The fork-drift figure is measured from the fork commit date to the manual date, not from a list of missing upstream fixes. Induced-demand evidence for Indian flyovers is largely expert opinion and press (Bengaluru), plus the IISc review; no before/after measured study was found.
documented_failures:
1. LANE-FREE-ONLY DESIGN (DhakaSim). Cause: built from scratch for Dhaka's non-lane traffic because VISSIM/MITSIM/SUMO were judged lane-based; the RoadBird paper states DhakaSim 'lacks the capability of simulating a lane-based structured traffic stream', so it could not compare lane vs non-lane designs and had to be extended into RoadBird. RoadBird's own results show neither paradigm dominates: non-lane is better on narrow roads with heterogeneous traffic, lane-based is better with homogeneous traffic, wide roads and high generation rates. Rule: support both lane-disciplined and lane-free behaviour per link (a laneDiscipline parameter/strip model), not one hard-coded paradigm.
2. FORK DRIFT (TrafficFluid-Sim). Cause: SUMO's lane-based core and TraCI socket latency pushed the team to fork SUMO (commit 6c09f092, 20 Oct 2020) and patch the internal car-following code; the May 2025 manual still targets that base, ships a Netedit executable 'tied to our version', and warns that editing the network in Netedit deletes their custom 'neigh lane' tags, which must be re-added by hand, and that many lane-based SUMO output variables are irrelevant or 'outright mishandled'. Rule: never fork a large engine in a 72-hour build; either use the upstream engine unmodified via its API, or own a small engine end to end. Keep custom data in your own schema, not as hand-injected tags in another tool's file format.
3. SIMULATOR GOING STALE (SiMTraM). Cause: IIT Bombay's heterogeneous-traffic extension of SUMO was released as a Windows binary (0.1.1) on SourceForge and last updated 2013-04-29; tied to an unspecified old SUMO version and a lab project, it was never folded upstream. Rule: publish source plus a pinned, reproducible build (lockfile, CI build, hosted demo) from day one, and keep India-specific behaviour as a separable module with its own tests.
4. STATIC PCU. Cause: Indo-HCM (2017) primarily uses static PCU factors to convert mixed traffic to car equivalents; studies report dynamic PCU, which varies with speed, flow and composition, describes flow-density with less scatter, and Indian authors argue dynamic values give more reliable design assessments. Caveat: one chapter finds dynamic PCU agrees well with the Indo-HCM saturation-flow method. Rule: simulate individual vehicle classes and report outputs per class and in vehicles; if PCU is shown, derive it from the simulation (area-occupancy or headway based) and label it, never hard-code a single static table as the capacity model.
5. NETWORK BOUNDARIES THAT HIDE DOWNSTREAM CONGESTION. Cause: FHWA guidance says the model must 'completely encompass all of the traffic congestion' in the influence area and that queues at the boundary mean the network should be extended. The IISc review of the 2026 Hebbal flyover/tunnel microsimulation found network-level analysis limited to the Mekhri Circle-Hebbal Junction link, a 'no spillover' recommendation with no supporting data, despite the report itself warning that both facilities could discharge onto the same downstream link. Rule: include at least one downstream junction beyond every proposal; measure queue at entry links and vehicles unable to enter (unserved demand) and flag any scenario where an entry or exit link is saturated.
6. LANE-BASED MODELS ON INDIAN ROADS. Cause: VISSIM, MITSIM and SUMO 'mainly focus on lane-based homogeneous' traffic (RoadBird); TrafficFluid authors say even SUMO's sublane model leaves the 'structural limitation of lanes' present; Indian VISSIM calibrations report that modifying default behavioural parameters is 'essential'. Rule: treat lateral position as a first-class state (strips or continuous) and calibrate defaults per class; do not ship default Western parameters.
7. INDUCED DEMAND AND SECOND-ORDER EFFECTS IGNORED IN FLYOVER STUDIES. Cause: the IISc review states mode share change, VKT growth and induced demand were 'not considered', diversion was set to arbitrary 50%/80% values copied from a tunnel DPR and applied to a flyover with different capacity, pier footprint reducing at-grade capacity was not modelled, and the intervention 'is pushing the point of congestion from one point to another'. Bengaluru flyover volume-capacity work (press) reported 8-10% traffic growth within a year. Rule: always offer a demand-response sensitivity (e.g. +10/+20% demand on the improved corridor) and model at-grade capacity loss under flyover piers; label results as fixed-demand.
8. UNVALIDATED DEMOS PRESENTED AS EVIDENCE. Cause: A/B Street was not calibrated to real volumes, so its author says results 'have to be met with much more skepticism' and critics dismissed it; RoadBird's validation used 63 Google Maps travel times (MAPE accuracy 82-95%); the Hebbal report did not disclose calibration parameters or data and its base-case speed (13.74 km/h) contradicted the DPR (4.29 km/h). Rule: display a persistent 'illustrative, not calibrated' badge unless a scenario is linked to a stated calibration dataset; report calibration target and error.
9. INCONSISTENT METRICS ACROSS SCENARIOS. Cause: Hebbal report gave travel time for 2027 but not 2047, delay for 2047 but not 2027, no queues or density at all; the reviewer says this makes comparison 'difficult, erroneous' and recommendations questionable; percentage improvements masked small absolute gains. Rule: compute the same fixed metric set for every scenario, show absolute and percentage deltas.
10. GRIDLOCK HIDDEN OR UNSOLVED. Cause: A/B Street vehicles got 'stuck. Like, permanently' on large maps due to broken intersection geometry, lane-changing quirks, poor signals and unrealistic demand, with 'only very modest success' fixing it; SUMO teleports vehicles stuck for 300 s by default and states grid-locks are 'rather common in congested simulation scenarios'. Rule: implement a deadlock detector, count and display stuck/teleported vehicles as a headline metric, never silently remove them.
11. SCOPE CREEP AND ABANDONMENT AFTER FUNDING/ENERGY ENDS. Cause: A/B Street scope 'way too broad', game-vs-planning-tool identity crisis, monolith sprawl, self-funding, no legal entity, 'Nobody's using it'; SiMTraM and DhakaSim lab projects stalled after their research cycle. Rule: one audience (planners/advocates exploring Indian junction and corridor proposals), one workflow, fixed feature list for 72 hours.
validation_approach: Each mistake was checked against a primary or near-primary source: RoadBird arXiv 2010.08590 full text (DhakaSim limitation, lane vs non-lane results, Google Maps validation); TrafficFluid-Sim user manual (May 2025) and SUMO Conference 2022 paper (fork commit and date, Netedit tag loss, TraCI and lane-based motivation); SiMTraM SourceForge page (last update 2013-04-29, binary only, GPLv3); A/B Street retrospective and gridlock design note (gridlock, no calibration, scope); SUMO teleport documentation; FHWA Traffic Analysis Toolbox Vol. III (boundary rule); IISc IST Lab technical review PDF (Hebbal: boundary, induced demand, metrics, calibration); PCU papers (static vs dynamic). Press items on Bengaluru flyovers are treated as secondary.
takeaway_for_our_build: Design rules for the 72-hour build: (1) One engine, owned end to end (custom TypeScript) or upstream SUMO used unmodified; no forks. (2) Per-link laneDiscipline so the same engine can run lane-based and lane-free/strip behaviour, and a built-in A/B toggle to compare them. (3) Vehicle classes simulated individually; any PCU shown is derived from the run, never a static input table. (4) Network presets must extend at least one junction downstream of every editable element; show entry-link queues and unserved demand; warn when queues reach the boundary. (5) Gridlock detector with stuck-vehicle count as a headline metric; no silent teleporting. (6) A demand sensitivity control (+/- % on corridor) and a fixed-demand warning on any flyover/capacity proposal; model capacity lost to piers/ramps at grade. (7) Same metric set for every scenario, absolute and percentage deltas, multiple seeds. (8) 'Illustrative, uncalibrated' badge by default, plus one documented sanity check (e.g. fundamental diagram or saturation flow per lane against an Indo-HCM-order-of-magnitude value) so the demo is not mistaken for evidence. (9) Source public with pinned, reproducible build and hosted static demo so it does not go stale like SiMTraM. (10) Narrow scope: planners/advocates testing Indian junction and corridor proposals; no game modes, no 3D, no city-wide OSM import in v1.
